# Regularized Low-Rank Approximations

## Masterclass on nonnegative LRA

### Lecture 1 — introduction and matrix low-rank models

---

## Summary of HDR contents

> I write this "Habilitation à Diriger des Recherches" (HDR) manuscript with the hope of demonstrating that regularized LRA (rLRA) is a rich topic with many exciting open questions. I also hope that fellow researchers who are willing to read through all this content will learn about some lesser-known results, tricks, and algorithmic details that can help them in their work on rLRA.

---

## Some personal context

- At age six, I enjoyed guessing the notes my piano tutor was playing while I was turning my back.
- I discovered that I could literally hear the label of the pitch class of individual notes.
- It was only later that I realized that music transcription is hard for everyone.
- In the end, the same mathematical concepts reappeared in low-rank approximations.

---

## Music, signal processing, and LRA

- I grew interested in sound, music processing, the Fourier transform, and their links to human perception.
- In my PhD, I realized that many problems in music information retrieval could be addressed using low-rank approximations.
- The design of regularizations and constraints was key to performance.
- This motivated my work on regularized LRA.

---

## A recurring theme

- Low-rank approximations are ubiquitous and critical in unsupervised machine learning.
- Though deep learning is stronger in some applications, LRA remains fundamental.
- Many applications, such as automatic music transcription, can still be improved with better LRA-based models.
- This is a field with exciting open questions.

---

## Why regularized low-rank approximations

- LRA are workhorse methods in several unsupervised machine learning tasks.
- They are used in dimensionality reduction and blind source separation.
- The most prominent example is Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

---

## Dimensionality reduction

- The reduction of dimension seeks to:
  - extract useful information from data;
  - compress data.
- These objectives often coincide: a good summary preserves useful information.

---

## Example: color perception by the human eye

- Materials reflect light with varying intensity across wavelengths.
- The spectral reflectance is a high-dimensional description.
- Human vision only sees three RGB channels.
- The infinite-dimensional spectrum is reduced to three coefficients.

---

![](../figures/Pca.png){fig-align="center" width="75%"}

## PCA as a projection model

A centered data matrix $M$ lies in a low-dimensional subspace $\operatorname{col}(U)$.

$$
M \approx U V^\top
$$

with $U$ encoding a basis and $V$ the coordinates.

---

## More formally

For matrix data, a real LRA problem is

$$
\min_{U \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\,V \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times r}} f(Y, U V^\top)
$$

where $r$ is the rank of the approximation and $r \ll m,n$.

Usually, $f(Y,X)=\|Y-X\|_F^2$.

---

## Matrix low-rank factorization

A low-rank model describes the columns of $M$ if they live in a smaller subspace.

$$
\exists\, U\in\mathbb{R}^{n_1\times r},\; V\in\mathbb{R}^{n_2\times r} \text{ such that } \forall j\le n_2,\; M[:,j] = UV^\top[:,j].
$$

The columns of $U$ form a basis of the low-dimensional space.

---

## Matrix rank and subspace dimension

- If the subspace dimension is minimal, it is the rank of matrix $M$.
- This is the smallest number $r$ such that $M$ is generated by $r$ basis vectors.
- The low-rank model reduces the dimension whenever $r \le \min(n_1,n_2)$.

---

## A second interpretation: sum of rank-one matrices

Another equivalent definition is

$$
M[i,j] = \sum_{q=1}^r U[i,q] V[j,q].
$$

Equivalently,

$$
M = \sum_{q=1}^{r} u_q v_q^\top.
$$

Each term is a rank-one matrix.

---

## Rank-one atoms

The roles of $U$ and $V$ are symmetric.

- $u_q$ and $v_q$ are the factors of the $q$-th rank-one component;
- matrix $M$ is a sum of $r$ such simple atoms;
- this is an atomic decomposition of the data.

---

## Rank as complexity

The rank of a matrix is a measure of its complexity.

- rank-one matrices are simple;
- full-rank matrices are more complicated;
- low-rank matrices can be summarized by a small number of atoms.

The model uses $(n_1+n_2)r$ parameters instead of $n_1n_2$.

---

## Low-rank approximations

In most real applications, data matrices are not exactly low-rank, but are well approximated by low-rank matrices.

A rank-$r$ approximation is the optimization problem

$$
\arg\min_{\operatorname{rank}(N)\le r} \|M-N\|_F^2.
$$

where

$$
\|M-N\|_F^2 = \sum_{i,j} (M_{ij}-N_{ij})^2.
$$

---

## Equivalent factorization form

The approximation can be parameterized by two factors:

$$
\arg\min_{U\in\mathbb{R}^{n_1\times r},\;V\in\mathbb{R}^{n_2\times r}} \|M - UV^\top\|_F^2.
$$

This is the Burer-Montero factorization.

---

## Exact low-rank factorization

The exact factorization problem is written as

$$
\text{Find } U\in\mathbb{R}^{n_1\times r},\;V\in\mathbb{R}^{n_2\times r}\text{ such that } M = UV^\top.
$$

This is often used as a conceptual model even when exact equality is impossible in practice.

---

## Frobenius norm and SVD

The Frobenius norm is the most common loss for LRA because it yields a closed-form solution.

Let

$$
M = A S B^\top
$$

be the singular value decomposition of $M$.

Then the optimal rank-$r$ approximation is obtained by the truncated SVD.

---

## Eckart-Young theorem

> Assume data matrix $M$ admits the singular value decomposition $M = A S B^\top$. Then
>
> $$
> \arg\min_{\operatorname{rank}(N)\le r}\|M-N\|_F^2
> $$
>
> admits the truncated SVD as a solution,
>
> $$
> N^\ast = A_{:,1:r} S_{1:r,1:r} B_{:,1:r}^\top.
> $$

The residual is exactly $\sum_{q=r+1}^{\min(n_1,n_2)} S_{q,q}^2$.

---

## Why this is so useful

- LRA in Frobenius norm is one of the rare nonconvex problems with a direct, efficient solution.
- The truncated SVD gives the optimal low-rank approximation under squared loss.
- This makes PCA and related models computationally attractive.

---

## But not all losses are the same

The same result holds for the spectral norm with a different residual, but for arbitrary loss functions, truncated SVD is generally not the solution.

A different loss often encountered in LRA is the KL divergence.

---

## Why are data matrices often approximately low-rank?

After years of research, one recurring phenomenon is striking:

- Many data matrices found in practice are approximately low-rank.
- There is no universal explanation, but several reasons exist.

---

## Reason 1: nice latent-variable models are low-rank

“Nice” latent variable models are often of low-rank form.

- For many generative models, the resulting data matrix is well approximated by a low-rank matrix.
- This observation is central in signal processing and machine learning.

---

## Reason 2: separable maps

The entries of a rank-one matrix are samples of a separable map:

$$
f(x,y) = f_1(x)f_2(y).
$$

This is common in physics because it gives a simple description of multivariate functions.

---

## Reason 3: source separation interpretation

Low-rank models can be interpreted as linear source separation models.

- rank is the number of underlying sources;
- $U$ contains source templates;
- $V$ contains mixing coefficients.

Nonlinearities, noise, and missing data corrupt the low-rank structure.

---

## Source-separation viewpoint

- In many applications, factor matrices have physical meaning.
- Practitioners often want LRA to recover the true underlying factors.
- This raises two central questions.

---

## Two key questions

1. Is the model essentially identifiable?
2. Is the estimation robust in the presence of noise?

These questions are essential when the factors are interpreted physically.

---

## Identifiability issue

The answer to the first question is negative in general.

If

$$
U_1 V_1^\top = U_2 V_2^\top,
$$

then the two bases may represent the same subspace, with

$$
U_1 = U_2 Q
$$

for some invertible matrix $Q$.

This is a fundamental rotation ambiguity.

---

## Trivial ambiguities in LRA

The main ambiguities are:

- scaling ambiguity: $ab^\top = \frac{1}{\lambda} a \cdot \lambda b^\top$;
- permutation ambiguity: $UV^\top = U\Pi\, (V\Pi)^\top$.

These are not harmful if we only care about the subspace.

---

## Essential uniqueness

> Essential uniqueness means uniqueness up to permutations and scalings.

This is the natural notion of identifiability for low-rank models.

It is often the best one can hope for when interpreting factors.

---

## Why regularization matters

The factor matrices may not be meaningful approximations of the true pair $(U^\ast, V^\ast)$ unless additional structure is imposed.

This motivates constrained or regularized LRA.

---

## Regularized LRA formulation

Regularized LRA can be written as

$$
\min_{U, V} f(Y,UV) + g_U(U) + g_V(V).
$$

The regularizers $g_U$ and $g_V$ promote properties such as:

- smoothness,
- sparsity,
- nonnegativity,
- physical constraints.

---

## Why regularization helps identifiability

A regularization on each factor separately is important because

$$
UV^\top = U P (V P)^\top
$$

still describes the same subspace for invertible $P$.

A regularizer on the product $UV^\top$ would not break this ambiguity.

---

## Nonnegative matrix factorization

A very important special case is NMF.

The exact NMF model is

$$
\text{Find } W\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n_1\times r},\; H\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n_2\times r}\text{ such that } M = W H^\top.
$$

This is a natural constraint when factors represent concentrations, spectra, probabilities, or similar nonnegative quantities.

---

## Approximate NMF

With squared Frobenius loss, approximate NMF solves

$$
\arg\min_{W\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n_1\times r},\;H\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n_2\times r}} \|M - W H^\top\|_F^2.
$$

Unlike unconstrained LRA, exact or approximate NMF does not generally admit closed-form solutions.

---

![](../figures/nmfmatrix.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

## NMF geometry

Nonnegative matrix factorization writes a nonnegative matrix as the product of two nonnegative factor matrices.

It is especially useful in source separation and pattern mining.

---

## NMF and physical meaning

In many applications, the factor matrices have a physical interpretation.

- matrix $W$ often stores templates;
- matrix $H$ stores activations or abundances;
- the model can reveal latent sources in the data.

---

## The hyperspectral example

![](../figures/Hsi_nmf.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

NMF performs spectral unmixing on hyperspectral images, identifying spectra and abundance maps.

---

## A central issue: can NMF be unique?

- Inverse problems require uniqueness to be interpretable.
- NMF is often not unique without additional structure.
- This motivates regularized NMF.

---

## Regularized NMF

There are at least three main regularization strategies.

1. separable NMF;
2. sparse NMF;
3. minimum-volume or maximum-volume NMF.

Each restricts the set of valid solutions.

---

## Separable NMF

The columns of $W$ are required to come from the columns of the data matrix $M$:

$$
M = M[:,\mathcal{K}] H^\top,
$$

where $\mathcal{K}$ is a subset of indices.

This drastically restricts the solution set and yields interpretable patterns.

---

## Sparse NMF

A typical sparse NMF objective is

$$
\arg\min_{W\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n_1\times r},\,H\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n_2\times r}} \|Y-WH^\top\|_F^2 + \lambda(\|W\|_F^2 + \|H\|_1).
$$

Sparse regularization pushes entries of $H$ toward zero and can encourage identifiability.

---

## Minimum-volume NMF

The idea is to choose the matrix $W$ to be as close as possible to the convex hull of the data.

A popular quantity is

$$
\log \det(W^\top W),
$$

which measures the volume of the cone spanned by $W$.

---

## Practical lesson

In many applications, regularized NMF should be considered instead of plain NMF.

- identifiability is not a minor technicality;
- it is central to interpretation and scientific validity;
- this matters especially in automatic transcription and other source-separation tasks.

---

## Conclusion of Lecture 1

- LRA is a central model in machine learning and signal processing.
- Low-rank approximations are powerful because they compress and reveal structure.
- PCA is the canonical example of a low-rank model with a closed-form solution.
- Regularization is needed when the factors are intended to have a physical meaning.
- Nonnegative LRA is a natural and important instance of this philosophy.
